# API reference

Generated from the source tree by `docs/make_api.py`. The public
surface is each module's `__all__`; anything else is internal and
is not listed here.

The names re-exported from the package root -- the ones in
`stabilis.__all__` -- are the stable API and will not move without
a version bump. They are marked **root** below. A name reached
through a submodule path may move.

| Page | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Core types and data handling](core.md) | Series types, provenance, the tau grid, editing and synthesis -- everything that is not itself an estimator. |
| [Reading and writing records](io.md) | Text and binary records in, records out, and the timebase they carry. |
| [Estimators, uncertainty and spectra](stats.md) | The variance family, confidence intervals, noise identification, power spectra and spurs. |
| [Several channels at once](multi.md) | Alignment, cross-variance, the N-cornered hat and the correlation matrix. |
| [Fitting a model to a curve](fitting.md) | Power-law and Gauss-Markov models fitted to a measured sigma-tau curve, with a covariance-aware uncertainty. |
| [Measurements that have not finished](stream.md) | Incremental estimation over a growing record, and dynamic stability. |
| [The measurement setup](bench.md) | Sources, devices and channels as a graph, and what that graph can and cannot determine. |
| [Getting results back out](export.md) | Sigma-tau tables, Stable32-shaped blocks and self-describing bundles. |
| [The measurement report](report.md) | The customer-facing HTML report and its conformity verdict. |
| [Validation machinery](validate.md) | The exact-rational oracle and the evidence report. |
| [Plotting](plot.md) | Matplotlib figures. Optional dependency, never required for a number. |
| [The local browser page](gui.md) | The request handling behind `stabilis gui`. |

| [`GAP_POLICIES`](stats.md#gap_policies) | constant | `stabilis.stats.core` | How a gap is allowed to affect the terms around it.  "mask"    -- keep the record whole; terms whose window touches a gap come back non-finite and are dropped. This assumes the timescale ran continuously across the gap, so the phase on either side is on one common origin. True for a dropped sample on a known grid; false after a counter reset. "segment" -- analyse each contiguous run on its own origin and pool the coefficients. Costs only the 2m (or 3m) terms spanning the gap. Required for frequency input, and correct for phase whose origin may have moved. "auto"    -- "segment" for frequency, "mask" for phase. |

Two-sided, because a deviance far *below* expectation is also a finding: it means the model has more freedom than the data can constrain, or the degrees of freedom are over-estimated. | [`HTOT_BIAS_MEASURED`](stats.md#htot_bias_measured) | constant | `stabilis.stats.bias` | HTOT's equivalent, measured the same way. **SP 1065 publishes no table** -- section 5.2.14 says only that "a bias correction is required that is dependent on the power law noise type and number of samples" and points at Howe et al., IEEE T-UFFC 52:1253 (2005), which is not in hand.  The three FM rows are the MTOT table shifted by two in alpha, to five significant figures, and that is not a coincidence: HTOT applies to the frequency record the operator MTOT applies to the phase, and S_x = S_y/(2 pi f)**2, so a y-noise of exponent alpha presents to it as an x-noise of alpha + 2. The two PM rows continue the sequence to alpha = 3 and 4, which the modified family has no counterpart for; they are also the two that still drift with m (white PM runs 0.741 to 0.723 over m = 8..64), so they are given at m = 32 and should be read as indicative. |

| [`implied_eta`](multi.md#implied_eta) | function | `stabilis.multi.cross` | `cross_sem` inverted: the degrees of freedom this error bar implies. |
| [`IMPULSE_TERMS`](validate.md#impulse_terms) | constant | `stabilis.validate.expected` | Terms of `h` retained. The recursion decays like k**(beta/2 - 1), so the steepest case this library generates (beta = 2, random-walk FM) does not decay at all and is the one that sets this: 2**16 terms put the residual of the checks below at 1e-11 relative, an order under the tightest tolerance any caller asserts at. |
| [`infer_rate`](io.md#infer_rate) | function | `stabilis.io.timebase` | `(rate_hz, jitter)` from timestamps, using the median interval. |
| [`INTEROP_RTOL`](core.md#interop_rtol) | constant | `stabilis.reference` | The published tables carry seven significant figures, so this is the tightest tolerance the data supports. Asserting harder would be asserting against digits the source never claimed. |
| [`isserlis_var`](stats.md#isserlis_var) | function | `stabilis.stats.isserlis` | Variance of the mean of the pair-averaged products, exactly. |
| [`J_MAX`](stats.md#j_max) | constant | `stabilis.stats.greenhall` | Truncation threshold for the full algorithm: past this many summands the closed-form integral replaces the sum. 100 is the paper's own suggestion (section 4.3), not a value tuned here. |
| [`KINDS`](core.md#kinds) | constant | `stabilis.registry` | "model" holds `fit.models.Model` records rather than bare callables. A model is five things -- the function, its parameter names, a starting guess, a description and which parameters are physically positive -- and a lookup that returned only the function would leave a plugin author unable to supply the other four. The registry is a name-to-thing dict; it does not care which thing. "writer" is the mirror of "reader" and holds the same sort of thing: a function that moves a data column between an array and a file. Result tables and report bundles are *not* writers in that sense -- they are the output layer, which is what the separate "report" kind is for. |
| [`KINDS`](stats.md#kinds) | constant | `stabilis.stats.psd` |  |
| [`KNOWN_DISCREPANCIES`](core.md#known_discrepancies) | constant | `stabilis.reference` | Published entries that disagree with our certified value.  **These are recorded, never edited away.** A reference table is evidence about what the incumbent produced. Overwriting an entry with a number this library computed turns an interoperability assertion into a statement about ourselves and destroys the only thing the table was for. Likewise nothing here may be interpolated, averaged, or filled in: a gap in a reference table is a gap, and the absence of a value is itself data about what has actually been checked.  Each entry declares how large the disagreement is relative to INTEROP_RTOL. A `rel` below it is a *source-quality note* -- the digit in question is finer than the table claims, so both values pass -- and does not exempt anything from the interop test. A `rel` above it would be a real conflict and is asserted to be absent.  (estimator, af): (published, certified, note)  Empty as of 2026-08-08, and the way it emptied is worth keeping.  The one entry here was 9-point hdev(1) = 70.80608, which disagreed with the oracle's 70.806073185850378 in the seventh figure. It was recorded rather than corrected, exactly as the rule requires. When SP 1065 Table 30 was finally read directly it turned out to print **70.80607** -- so the handbook and the oracle had agreed all along and the disagreement belonged to the intermediate source.  That is the case *for* the rule, not against it. Had the entry been quietly rewritten to match our own output when it was first noticed, the agreement found later would have proved nothing, because it would have been an agreement we had manufactured. Leaving it alone kept the question open until primary evidence could close it. |

| [`MAX_BIAS_OPS`](stats.md#max_bias_ops) | constant | `stabilis.stats.theoh` | Ceiling on the element-operations the bias ratio may cost, past which `theobr` refuses rather than appearing to hang. Measured throughput here is about 1.2e8 of these per second (8.7 s at N = 4097, where the sum costs 1.06e9), so this is roughly half a minute, reached at around N = 6500 phase points. The cost grows as N^3, so the next octave of record length is eight times the wait. |
| [`MAX_COLUMNS`](io.md#max_columns) | constant | `stabilis.io.text` |  |
| [`MAX_GAP_SAMPLES`](stream.md#max_gap_samples) | constant | `stabilis.stream.collect` | Longest run of missing samples that will be materialized as NaN. |
| [`MAX_GRID_OFFSET_SAMPLES`](multi.md#max_grid_offset_samples) | constant | `stabilis.multi.align` | How far an epoch may sit off the common grid, in samples. This is a float64 slop allowance and nothing more: an MJD-scale epoch resolves to about 6e-7 s, so exact equality is unattainable while 1e-3 of a sample is unreachable by any real misalignment. Anything larger is a genuine sub-sample offset, which no crop can fix. |
| [`MAX_RING_BYTES`](stream.md#max_ring_bytes) | constant | `stabilis.stream.online` | Ceiling on the phase history one accumulator may hold. The ring is `2*max(af)+1` float64, so this is a direct bound on the largest averaging factor a stream may track -- about 16 million at the default. It is a memory bound rather than a preference, and it is stated because the alternative is a process killed by the allocator, which is not an error the code gets to report. |
| [`MAX_SLIP_SAMPLES`](multi.md#max_slip_samples) | constant | `stabilis.multi.align` | How far the records may drift apart over the cropped window, in samples, before the rates count as different. Half a sample is the point at which a term in one record is nearer a *neighbouring* term in the other than to its own partner, so the pairing itself has become wrong rather than merely imprecise. |
| [`MAX_TAUS`](core.md#max_taus) | constant | `stabilis.tau` | Hard ceiling on how many averaging factors any grid may produce.  **This is a memory bound, not a taste one.** Each averaging factor keeps a coefficient array of order `n` for the confidence-interval path, so the cost is `n_taus * n`. An unbounded `all` grid on a 200 000-point record asks for 50 000 factors and 60 GB, and the process is killed rather than slowed; at a million points it is 1500 GB. Nothing warns, because running out of memory is not an error the code gets to report. |
| [`MAX_WINDOWS`](stream.md#max_windows) | constant | `stabilis.stream.davar` | Ceiling on how many windows one call may evaluate. Each is a full batch run, so the cost is linear in this and a default `step` on a long record can ask for a great many. The message names `step`, which is the knob. |

| [`MIN_FH_TAU_PRODUCT`](core.md#min_fh_tau_product) | constant | `stabilis.powerlaw_coeffs` | A row is used only where `2*pi*f_h*tau` clears this. The conversions are asymptotic in that product, and SP 1065 states they "can be applied only when the dominant noise process decreases toward higher sideband frequencies". Ten is the conventional floor; below it the coefficient is not merely imprecise but wrong in a way no error bar reports. |
| [`MIN_TERMS_FOR_ETA1`](stats.md#min_terms_for_eta1) | constant | `stabilis.stats.edof` | Below this many terms the sample autocorrelation is mostly noise and eta1 stops being informative -- it can even exceed M. Fall back to eta3, which is conservative by construction and cannot mislead in the optimistic direction. The threshold is deliberately generous; long tau is exactly where an over-narrow error bar does the most damage. |

| [`MTOT_BIAS_MEASURED`](stats.md#mtot_bias_measured) | constant | `stabilis.stats.bias` | The same ratio measured here: 400 realizations at N = 2048, ensemble mean of MVAR over ensemble mean of MTOT, at m = 8, 16, 32, 64. Flat in m over that range and flat in N from 256 to 4096, which is SP 1065's own claim that the factor is "essentially independent of the averaging factor and number of data points".  **Flicker PM agrees exactly and white FM to 2%; white PM, flicker FM and random-walk FM disagree by 5%, 7% and 12%.** The estimator is not in doubt -- `allantools.mtotdev` returns our numbers to every printed digit, which is two independent readings of eq. (27) agreeing. What is in doubt is whether Stable32 computes eq. (27) or something slightly different, and only the Stable32 session settles that. Recorded, not reconciled: see theory/mtotal.md and VALIDATION-DEBT. |
| [`MTOT_BIAS_PUBLISHED`](stats.md#mtot_bias_published) | constant | `stabilis.stats.bias` | SP 1065 Table 11, transcribed. Its caption reads "the ratio of the expected value of Mod Totvar to MVAR", and section 5.12 says "this bias factor should be used to correct all reported MTOT results".  **The caption's direction is inverted relative to its own values.** Measured here, MTOT is biased *low* against MVAR for every noise type but white PM, so E[MTOT]/MVAR runs 0.68 to 1.00 and it is the reciprocal that lands on this table. Read as a multiplier -- MTOT times this is an estimate of MVAR -- the values are what "correct all reported MTOT results" has to mean, and that is how `mtot_bias` returns it. |

| [`MVAR_FLICKER_FM_COEFF`](core.md#mvar_flicker_fm_coeff) | constant | `stabilis.powerlaw_coeffs` | Mod AVAR for flicker FM, as a pure number: `Mod sigma2_y = K * h_-1`.  Derived, not transcribed, and the only coefficient here with no closed form. Quadrature of SP 1065 eq. (66) gives K(m) = 0.9352449 at m=128, 0.9352320 at 256, 0.9352288 at 512, 0.9352280 at 1024, converging as 1/m**2 to the value below. A search over `a*ln2 + b*ln3` with small rational a, b found nothing within 2e-9, so the number is shipped as a number with its derivation rather than dressed up as a closed form it does not have. `27*ln(2)/20 = 0.9357487` is close and is **not** it -- it misses in the fourth figure, well outside the quadrature's own convergence. |

Detected by the result's `is_variance` flag, not by name, so an estimator this module has never heard of is still caught. The names are kept only for the error message. |
| [`REFUSED_KINDS`](bench.md#refused_kinds) | constant | `stabilis.bench.solve` | Statistics that are not variances, detected by the result's own `is_variance` flag rather than by name so a plugin estimator cannot slip past. The names below are for the error message only.  The two this library ships fail for *different* reasons, and saying "extreme-value statistics" of both would be wrong. MTIE is one: the maximum of a sum is not the sum of maxima. TIE rms is a mean square and its stochastic part does obey the sum rule -- it is refused because it retains the frequency offset between the sources, which is deterministic, so two clocks 1e-12 off can differ by 2e-12 or by nothing depending on sign. Neither combines the way this solver assumes. |

| [`SLOPES`](plot.md#slopes) | constant | `stabilis.plot` | sigma_y(tau) ~ tau**exponent for each power law. The deviation slope is half the variance slope: AVAR goes as tau**(-alpha-1) for -2 <= alpha <= 0 and saturates at tau**-2 for both PM noises, so the deviation slopes are these. White PM and flicker PM share tau**-1 -- that they are indistinguishable here is the same degeneracy `powerlaw.py` stacks modified rows to break, and drawing them as one line says so honestly. |

| [`THEO1_BIAS_MEASURED`](stats.md#theo1_bias_measured) | constant | `stabilis.stats.bias` | Thêo1's bias against AVAR, at the same tau, for m >~ 100.  **Measured here, not published.** 60 realizations at N=8192 of each power law, Thêo1 against an interpolated overlapping AVAR at Thêo1's own tau. White FM comes out at 1.00, which is the property that identified the missing 0.75 in SP 1065 eq. (30) -- see stats/theo1.py. The FM biases are real and are what Howe's TheoBR exists to remove by averaging Thêo1 against AVAR over the range where both are defined.  TheoBR is not implemented, so these are here to be *reported*, not silently applied: a number divided by a ratio measured on synthetic noise is not the same thing as a number corrected by a published estimator. |

Published, unlike THEO1_BIAS_MEASURED below -- which is why both are here. White FM is the (1, 0, 0) row, the identity that identified the missing 0.75 in eq. (30). |
